steps.text: Connect the object to the negative terminal; it is the cathode.
Cathode: Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu.
Anode: Cu→Cu²⁺+2e⁻.

An inert anode does not supply Cu²⁺ by dissolving, so copper deposition removes Cu²⁺ without that replenishment.

verification.method: Author derivation and automated schema, rendering and numerical checks
verification.notes: Original practice for the first-assessment-2025 syllabus. Marking points are instructional; equivalent chemically valid explanations and appropriate error-carried-forward working are accepted. Separate human examiner moderation has not been performed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name and give the condensed formula of the main organic product targeted in each experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the different outcomes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State the main oxidation product of propan-2-ol and explain why the same simple route does not yield propanoic acid.

steps.text: Distillation targets propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO.
Reflux with excess oxidant targets propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.
Distillation removes the aldehyde from contact with oxidant, limiting further oxidation.
Reflux returns volatile material and allows the aldehyde to undergo further oxidation to the acid.
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃.
The secondary alcohol forms a ketone; conversion to a carboxylic acid would require carbon–carbon bond cleavage rather than the analogous aldehyde oxidation step.

title: A radical chain for ethane
stem: Ethane reacts with chlorine under ultraviolet light to form chloroethane and hydrogen chloride.

verification.method: Author derivation and automated schema, rendering and numerical checks
verification.notes: Original practice for the first-assessment-2025 syllabus. Marking points are instructional; equivalent chemically valid explanations and appropriate error-carried-forward working are accepted. Separate human examiner moderation has not been performed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the initiation step and explain the bond-cleavage type.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write two propagation steps that regenerate a chlorine radical.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write a termination step that forms butane and explain why it is termination.

steps.text: Cl₂→2Cl·, with UV light indicated.
Homolytic cleavage sends one electron from the Cl–Cl bond to each atom, giving two radicals.
Cl·+C₂H₆→HCl+C₂H₅·.
C₂H₅·+Cl₂→C₂H₅Cl+Cl·.
C₂H₅·+C₂H₅·→C₄H₁₀.
Two radicals are consumed and no radical is produced.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Give the two possible monochlorinated constitutional isomers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons why the actual product mixture may be more complicated than these two substances.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest how the relative amount of multiple substitution can be reduced without claiming a perfectly pure product.

steps.text: 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl.
2-chloropropane, CH₃CHClCH₃.
Chlorinated products still contain C–H bonds and can undergo further substitution to form multiply chlorinated products.
Radicals can combine in different termination steps, including carbon–carbon coupling. Accept another chemically distinct, valid termination-derived product explanation.
Use a large excess of propane relative to chlorine, limiting further chlorination of already substituted molecules.

parts.prompt: Describe the two curly arrows required in the single step, including their origins and destinations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give the products and describe the key features of the transition state.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a free ethyl carbocation should not be drawn as an intermediate in this specified mechanism.

steps.text: One arrow starts at an oxygen lone pair of OH⁻ and ends at the carbon bonded to Br.
The second starts at the C–Br bond and ends on Br, transferring the bonding pair to the leaving group.
CH₃CH₂OH and Br⁻.
The nucleophile attacks opposite the leaving group; C–O bond formation and C–Br bond breaking occur simultaneously with partial bonds in the transition state.
SN2 is concerted and has no carbocation intermediate; such an intermediate would describe a different pathway.

title: A two-step substitution pathway
stem: A tertiary halogenoalkane, $(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}$, undergoes substitution by an SN1 route with hydroxide as nucleophile in a simplified mechanism.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Show the first step using an equation and describe the required curly arrow.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the subsequent nucleophile attack and give the product.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a tertiary carbocation is generally more stable than a primary carbocation.

steps.text: $(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}\rightarrow(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C^+}+\mathrm{Br^-}$.
Arrow starts at the C–Br bond and ends on Br; the bond cleaves heterolytically.
An oxygen lone pair of OH⁻ attacks the positively charged carbon, forming a C–O bond.
The product is (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Alkyl groups donate electron density and help disperse/stabilize the positive charge.
A tertiary centre has three alkyl groups providing this stabilization, compared with one at a primary centre.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the major product and the more stable carbocation leading to it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the arrows in the first step and in the bromide-attack step.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the origin of the major-product preference.

steps.text: 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃.
The secondary carbocation CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ is favoured over the primary alternative.
The π bond donates an electron pair to H of H–Br; the H–Br bond pair moves to Br.
A bromide lone pair then forms a bond to the positively charged carbon.
The route through the better-stabilized secondary carbocation is favoured; alkyl groups help stabilize the positive charge.

stem: Benzene reacts with a supplied electrophile $\mathrm{E^+}$ to form $\mathrm{C_6H_5E}$. You do not need to describe how E⁺ is generated.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe how the final product forms, including the role of a base.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why substitution is favoured over a final addition product in this model.

steps.text: A curly arrow starts from the ring π electron system and ends at E⁺, forming a C–E bond.
The intermediate is a positively charged, non-aromatic sigma complex; continuous ring delocalization is temporarily disrupted.
A base accepts the proton on the carbon bonded to E.
The C–H bond pair returns to the ring to restore the π system and aromatic delocalization.
Substitution restores the stabilizing delocalized aromatic system; a simple addition product would leave that stabilization disrupted.

steps.text: Total charge=+3+5(0)−1=+2.
Coordination number=6, because six donor atoms bond directly to cobalt.
Ammonia is the Lewis base: its nitrogen lone pair is donated.
The cobalt centre is the Lewis acid: it accepts the pair to form a coordinate covalent bond.
The resulting complex has charge +3, because a −1 ligand is replaced by a neutral ligand.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine pKa and Ka from the half-equivalence point.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Check whether the 20.00 cm³ reading is consistent with this pKa.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the approximate effect of doubling the volume of this buffer with water.

steps.text: At half-equivalence [HA]=[A⁻], so [H⁺]=Ka and pH=pKa.
Before equivalence, A⁻:HA=20.00:(25.00−20.00)=4:1.
pH=4.80+log₁₀4=5.40, consistent with the data.
Both conjugate components are diluted by the same factor, so their ratio and approximate pH remain unchanged; the buffer capacity per unit volume decreases.
